# Introduction

Allometric equations are the foundation of forest biomass and carbon estimation. Because destructive measurement is impractical at operational scale, inventories convert measured tree dimensions, principally diameter at breast height (DBH), into component and total biomass through fitted allometric relationships, and every reported carbon stock ultimately rests on that conversion [@vorster2020]. The equations used for this purpose vary in taxonomic and geographic scope, from local, species-specific models built for a single site to generalized regional and national models intended for application across many species and conditions. Generalized national equations, such as Canada's national biomass equations [@lambert2005; @ung2008], exist precisely because local destructive equations are unavailable for most species and places. Fitted to thousands of trees and constrained so that components sum to total biomass, they provide internally consistent, transferable estimates at the national scale, and for that reason they are embedded in national carbon accounting and in operational provincial inventories.

That generality carries a recognized and accepted cost. Pooling across species and regions to gain consistency reduces accuracy and widens prediction uncertainty for populations under-represented in the calibration data. The magnitude of this trade-off has been measured directly. In west-central Canada, average prediction error rose from 9 to 12 to 25 kg per tree as equations generalized from local to regional to national, and national equations were statistically indistinguishable from local ones for only five of ten species [@case2008]. In northwestern Alberta, the diameter-based national equations underestimated aboveground biomass for white spruce while the diameter-and-height forms overestimated aspen and underestimated spruce [@xing2019]. Allometric equation choice is not a minor term in the error budget: it contributes between 30 and 75 percent of total uncertainty in landscape biomass maps, rivalling or exceeding remote-sensing model error [@vorster2020; @ahmed2013]. These findings do not indict generalized equations, which perform acceptably for most species; they establish that the size of the trade-off is species- and context-specific and must be evaluated where a population departs from the calibration norm.

Two features of that trade-off are central to the present study. First, whole-tree accuracy can conceal component-level bias. In eastern Canadian open woodlands the national equations predicted whole-tree aboveground biomass of black spruce and jack pine accurately yet underestimated the branch component, a bias attributable to a crown form atypical of the closed-canopy stands that dominate the calibration [@fradette2021]. In western Canadian peatlands the national model underestimated the total biomass of small, stunted black spruce by roughly twelve percent, and a stratum-specific model removed most of that bias [@wagers2024]. Component-resolved larch studies show the same logic: fitting separate equations for stem wood, stem bark, branches, and foliage reveals departures from existing equations that a total-biomass comparison would miss [@delcourt2022]. Second, bias concentrates where morphology or size departs from the calibration population. Because component biomass follows a power function of diameter, error is largest for trees whose form, or whose diameter, lies at or beyond the range and central tendency of the calibration sample.

Western larch (*Larix occidentalis*) is an unusually clear case of both departures. It is a deciduous conifer, shade-intolerant, among the fastest-growing and most fire-resistant trees of the northwestern montane forests, and it attains large diameters well into the tail of, or beyond, the diameter range of typical national calibration samples. Its crown architecture is atypical of the evergreen conifers that dominate that calibration: foliage scales nearly linearly with diameter and is distributed diffusely through a long crown rather than concentrating as the crown lengthens [@williams2017], and larch foliage allometry further depends on stand structure and species admixture [@dirnberger2017]. Most relevant here, western larch develops among the thickest bark of any North American conifer, an adaptation to frequent low-intensity fire. Thick bark makes stem bark a substantial and size-increasing fraction of stem mass rather than a minor pool, and because bark thickness increases with tree size, any mismatch between a larch bark relationship and a coefficient calibrated largely on thinner-barked conifers should widen with diameter and concentrate in the large trees that hold most of a stand's biomass and carbon. Bark is also consequential for carbon in its own right: it is dense, persistent, and slow to decompose, and it enters volume-to-biomass conversion and harvest-residue accounting.

The operational stakes are concrete in British Columbia, where western larch is commercially and ecologically important through the interior and the Interior Wetbelt. Carbon estimates there are produced with generalized inventory and national allometric tools, and the errors of those tools are material: in the Interior Wetbelt, the operational Vegetation Resources Inventory underestimated field-measured carbon by as much as seventy-five percent in the densest stands [@dellasala2022], and national-scale biomass products continue to be evaluated and revised against independent plot data [@tompalski2026]. Quantifying and, where warranted, correcting a component-level bias in a major, biomass-dominant pool of a commercially important species is therefore directly relevant to credible carbon accounting.

Despite this, the adequacy of the national stem-bark coefficient for western larch has not been evaluated, nor has the way its error scales with diameter, nor the consequence of any such error for stand-level carbon. It is not even established whether western larch is represented by a species-specific national bark coefficient or is estimated through a pooled or borrowed one, a distinction that itself bears on the expected bias. We address this gap using destructively sampled western larch that span the operational diameter range, including the large trees where the trade-off should be greatest.

Our objective is to quantify the bias and uncertainty of the national stem-bark coefficient for western larch across the operational diameter range, and to determine whether a species-specific bark coefficient is warranted. We test the following hypotheses:

- **H1.** The national stem-bark coefficient underestimates observed stem-bark biomass in western larch, because western larch bark exceeds the thickness of the conifers that dominate the national calibration.
- **H1a (size dependence).** The underestimation increases with tree diameter and is greatest in large trees, reflecting the size increase of bark thickness in this fire-adapted species and the extrapolation of the national relationship toward and beyond its calibration diameter range.
- **H1b (uncertainty).** A species-specific bark coefficient reduces prediction uncertainty, expressed as relative root mean square error, relative to the national coefficient.
- **H1c (stand-level consequence).** Because large trees dominate stand biomass, the component-level bark bias propagates to a non-negligible bias in stand-level bark carbon.

The corresponding null position is that the national coefficient is unbiased across the diameter range and that a species-specific coefficient offers no reduction in uncertainty, in which case the national coefficient is adequate for western larch bark and no correction is warranted. Establishing which of these holds, and over what part of the size distribution, is the contribution of this paper.
